=== Tesla, Inc. Comments on Proposed PFP in Project 58481.pdf ===
                                   PUC PROJECT NO. 58481

RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                          §       PUBLIC UTILICY COMMISSION
LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                       §               OF TEXAS
STANDARDS UNDER PURA § 37.0561                   §


                                  TESLA, INC.’S COMMENTS

   I.       INTRODUCTION

         Tesla, Inc. (“Tesla”) appreciates the opportunity to comment on Project 58481 Rulemaking
to Implement Large Load Interconnection Standards Under PURA §37.0561. Under SB 6, the
Commission is directed to establish standards for interconnecting large load customers “in a
manner designed to support business development in this state while minimizing the potential for
stranded infrastructure costs and maintaining system reliability.” We appreciate the Commission’s
and Staff’s efforts to contend with speculative load and to strike a balance between the interests
described in SB 6. However, while it is reasonable for large loads to provide financial securities as
means of disciplining speculative interconnection applications and paying for incurred
interconnection and system upgrade costs, the draft Proposal for Publication (PFP) also requires
substantial, redundant, non-refundable financial obligations that could deter economic
development and investment in lieu of a more appropriately targeted protection against stranded
infrastructure costs. Instead, Tesla supports a consolidated financial security framework, in which
all or nearly all posted amounts are applied to actual costs related to interconnecting projects.

         As a substantial manufacturer and grid solutions provider in Texas, Tesla's facilities
operations include: Gigafactory Texas in Austin, a large facility that houses vehicle manufacturing
operations, an AI data center and a co-located Tesla Megapack battery energy storage system
(BESS); a lithium refinery near Corpus Christi; a growing network of EV fast-charging sites
statewide; and construction of a large Megafactory to produce Megapack in Brookshire, Texas,
near Houston. Tesla also has significant experience in the deployment of Megapack battery BESS
installations co-located with industrial facilities and data centers across the United States.

   II.      FINANCIAL SECURITIES AND FEES

         The latest draft PFP requires large load customers to post $50,000/MW financial security
due at the time that the intermediate agreement is executed, a non-refundable $50,000/MW
interconnection fee, a financial security for significant equipment or services due prior to the
                                                                                            Page 1 of 3
 interconnection agreement being executed, contribution in aid of construction (CIAC) to cover
direct interconnection costs due prior to the interconnection agreement being executed, and
financial security for system upgrades also due prior to the date that the interconnection agreement
is executed. These requirements ask large load customers to post multiple and sometimes
overlapping securities, while also forfeiting other funds outright even if the customer pays for all
project interconnection costs, system network costs, and energizes.

          Instead, Tesla supports a consolidated financial security framework, in which all posted
amounts are applied to actual project costs by applying the $50,000/MW intermediate agreement
financial security on a dollar-for-dollar basis to obligations for interconnection equipment,
services, and CIAC. We are largely supportive of the proposal submitted by Intersect Power, LLC,
which recommends such a consolidated framework. Notably, we are supportive of changes to
remove the non-refundable interconnection fee in favor of a consolidated, creditable financial
security. A non-refundable interconnection fee is inconsistent with principles of cost causation
given that it is paid over and above financial securities covering equipment, service, construction,
and system network costs, which themselves serve to cover any potential risk of stranded grid
infrastructure costs in line with SB 6. A consolidated financial security framework would take a
customer’s significant security deposit paid at the time that the intermediate agreement is executed
and apply the deposit to other project costs and financial postings as the customer moves through
the interconnection process. Importantly, large load customers would still be on the hook for all
project-related interconnection and system upgrade costs, protecting ratepayers while not deterring
economic investment in Texas.

   III.      CONCLUSION

          We believe that these proposed modifications will help better achieve the balance between
minimizing potential for stranded infrastructure costs, maintaining system reliability, and
supporting business development. Tesla appreciates the opportunity to provide these comments.

                                                      Respectfully submitted,

                                                      /s/ Jordan Graham
                                                      Jordan Graham
                                                      Manager, North America Energy Policy
                                                      Tesla, Inc.
                                                      jordgraham@tesla.com

LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                         §             OF TEXAS
STANDARDS UNDER PURA § 37.0561                     §



            EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF TESLA, INC. COMMENTS ON PFP

•   Tesla appreciates the Commission’s and Staff’s efforts to contend with speculative load and to
    strike a balance between the interests described in SB 6: minimizing potential for stranded
    infrastructure costs, maintaining system reliability, and supporting business development.

•   We oppose the proposal of a non-refundable interconnection fee on top of other financial
    securities and obligations. It is reasonable for large loads to provide financial securities as
    means of disciplining speculative interconnection applications and paying for incurred
    interconnection and system upgrade costs. However, a sizable non-refundable fee could deter
    economic development and investment. We support a more appropriately targeted protection
    against stranded infrastructure costs.

•   We recommend a consolidated financial security framework, in which all posted amounts are
    applied to actual project costs by applying the $50,000/MW intermediate agreement financial
    security on a dollar-for-dollar basis to obligations for interconnection equipment, services, and
    CIAC. We recommend removing the non-refundable interconnection fee in favor of a
    consolidated, creditable financial security.
